title: Identification of Mycobacterial genes that alter growth and pathology in macrophages and in mice.
text_summary: 研究者筛选结核分枝杆菌转座子突变库，发现相邻的cyp125、fadE28和fadE29等基因所在区域与宿主细胞损伤有关，并将包含6个基因的区域命名为igr。删除igr区域后，菌株对巨噬细胞的毒性和细胞内增殖能力显著下降，互补菌株可恢复表型；在活化巨噬细胞中野生型与突变株的差异减小。小鼠气溶胶感染显示突变株早期肺内生长滞后、向脾脏播散延迟且肺部病理减轻，但长期持续存在能力未明显改变。该区域可能通过脂质代谢相关功能促进结核感染早期的细胞内生存和致病过程。

MAJOR ARTICLE
Identiﬁcation of Mycobacterial Genes That Alter
Growth and Pathology in Macrophages and in Mice
Jennifer C. Chang, 1,a Nada S. Harik, 2,a Reiling P . Liao,1,a and David R. Sherman 1,a
1Department of Pathobiology and 2Division of Pediatric Infectious Diseases, University of Washington, Seattle
Mycobacterium tuberculosis lives intracellularly, and many facets of its interactions with host cells are not well
understood. W e screened an M. tuberculosis transposon library for mutants exhibiting reduced ability to kill
eukaryotic cells. Four of the mutants identiﬁed had insertions in 3 adjacent genes: single insertions in each
of 2 acyl–coenzyme A dehydrogenases (fadE) plus 2 unique insertions in a cytochrome P450 homolog. A
mutant in which these genes were replaced by allelic exchange was powerfully attenuated in our macrophage
viability assay, and there was a striking defect in its ability to grow intracellularly. Interestingly, the difference
between wild-type and mutant growth was minimized in activated macrophages. Aerosol infection of mice
revealed a lag in growth, delayed dissemination to the spleen, and reduced lung pathology but no difference
in persistence. Thus, these genes may be particularly important for events early during infection.
Despite more than a century of research, Mycobacte-
rium tuberculosis (MTB) continues to challenge global
public health. MTB infects roughly one-third of the
world’s population [1] and kills nearly 2 million per-
sons annually [2]. Several issues complicate the pre-
vention and treatment of tuberculosis, including an in-
effective vaccine, extended chemotherapy regimens,
drug resistance, and synergy with HIV . We need to
understand the pathogenesis of MTB infection so that
better strategies to ﬁght it can be designed.
As an intracellular pathogen, MTB faces unique chal-

lenges in acquiring nutrients and resisting host defenses.
Metals, amino acids, purines, pyrimidines, and cofac-
tors may be limited in the host environment [3–9]. In
addition, little is known about the energy sources used
by mycobacteria during infection, although host lipids
are a likely resource [10–14], and the MTB genome
contains ∼ 5 times more genes devoted to lipid metab-
olism than does that of Escherichia coli [15]. MTB pro-
duces a remarkably diverse and abundant array of
lipids, and some of these have been implicated in path-
ogenesis [16, 17]. However, the precise mechanisms by
which these compounds regulate phagocyte function
and adaptive immunity and/or contribute directly to
resistance to oxidative stress are, for the most part, not
well understood.
In the present study, we identiﬁed a region of the
MTB genome that is important for intracellular survival
and has a possible function in lipid catabolism. This
region has been previously identiﬁed by microarray
studies as being up-regulated in macrophages [18] and
required for survival in macrophages [19] and mice
[20]. We have performed a more-detailed investigation
into the role these genes play in infection and have
renamed the region “igr” for the defect in intracellular
growth. Our studies with cultured macrophages and
mice indicate that these genes affect mycobacterial
growth in vivo in complex ways.

MATERIALS AND METHODS
Bacterial strains and growth conditions. Mycobacteria were
grown at 37 /H11034C in Middlebrook 7H9 medium supplemented
with 0.05% Tween 80 and albumin, dextrose, and catalase
(ADC; Becton Dickinson) or on Middlebrook 7H10 plates sup-
plemented with oleic acid and ADC, unless otherwise indicated.
Strains were stored as 1-mL aliquots in 15% glycerol at /H1100280/H11034C.
E. coli strains XL-1 Blue (Stratagene) and DH5-a (Invitrogen)
were used for cloning. Kanamycin and hygromycin were used
at 33 and 50 mg/mL, respectively, for mycobacteria, or at 50
and 150 mg/mL, respectively, for E. coli.
Generation of transposon mutant library. H37Rv:Dregion
of difference (RD) 1 [21] was mutagenized with MycoMarT7
phage as described elsewhere [22]. Brieﬂy, bacteria at an OD
600
of ∼ 1.0 were infected with ∼ phages for 3 h at 37 /H11034C103 /H1100310
and then plated on selective medium. After 3 weeks, individual
mutants were transferred to 7H9 medium in 96-well plates,
grown for 7 days, and then stored at 4 /H11034C. Before THP-1 in-
fection, each 96-well plate was replicated onto 7H10. T o identify
the site of transposon insertion, arbitrary primer polymerase
chain reaction (PCR) was performed [23, 24]. PCR products
were sequenced and compared with the H37Rv genome.
Preparation of macrophages. Human THP-1 cells were
maintained in RPMI 1640 and l-glutamine (Invitrogen) sup-
plemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS) and penicillin-
streptomycin at 37 /H11034Ci n5 %C O
2. Then, 72 h before infection,
cells were differentiated with PMA (Sigma), seeded at a density
of cells/well (96-well plates) or cells/well (24-
458 /H1100310 5 /H1100310
well plates) in antibiotic-free medium, and allowed to adhere.
Next, 24 h before infection, monolayers were washed and given
fresh medium. J774A.1 murine macrophages were maintained
in Dulbecco’s modiﬁed Eagle medium, high glucose, l-gluta-
mine, and NaPyr (Invitrogen) supplemented with 10% FBS
and were seeded into 24-well plates at a density of cells/
51 /H1100310
well. J774A.1 cells were activated with 30 U/mL interferon
(IFN)–g (Calbiochem) and 10 ng/mL lipopolysaccharide (LPS;
Sigma).
Macrophage infections. T o screen the transposon library,
mutants in 96-well plates were resuspended, and 2mL of culture
were added to THP-1 monolayers. After 4 h, cells were washed
and returned to 37 /H11034C. At day 5, medium was replaced with
150 mL of RPMI, FBS, and 10% Alamar Blue (Biosource In-
ternational). Plates were examined visually after 8 h; pink wells
(indicating viable THP-1 cells) were noted. Bacterial strains
were transferred from corresponding wells on master plates,
and phenotypes were validated in a 24-well Alamar Blue assay
as described elsewhere [21, 24]. T o quantify intracellular growth
in THP-1 and J774A.1 macrophages, monolayers were infected
at an MOI of 0.1. At each time point, monolayers were lysed
with 0.015% SDS, and serial dilutions were plated on 7H10.
RNA analyses. MTB RNA was prepared from macrophages
infected as described elsewhere [25]. Brieﬂy, THP-1 cells
73 /H1100310
were infected for 12 h (MOI of 10); then cells were washed,
and medium was replaced. After 24 h, monolayers were lysed
with 20 mL of Trizol (Invitrogen) and centrifuged at 3300 g
for 20 min to pellet bacteria. Supernatants were discarded, and
MTB RNA from the pellets was prepared as described elsewhere
[26], except that samples were reextracted with Trizol LS (In-
vitrogen) after the ﬁrst DNase (Promega) treatment and were
DNased again before reverse transcription. cDNA was synthe-
sized from 1 mg of total RNA primed with JC96, which anneals
at the distal end of igrF, in reactions with and without Ther-
moscript (Invitrogen) for 60 min at 50 /H11034C. cDNA was diluted
before PCR to amplify products speciﬁc to igrAB (163 bp), igrC
(232 bp), and igrF (106 bp); for primers, see table 1.
Deletion of the igr operon. The genes Rv3540c–Rv3545c
were replaced by allelic exchange as described elsewhere [21,
26] to create the strain H37Rv: Digr. H37Rv:Digr is kanamycin
sensitive because of a single base substitution in aph resulting
in a premature stop; interestingly, the kanamycin selection works
in E. coli, possibly because of the strains’ supE44 genotype.
Construction of the pJC52 complementation vector. A
PCR-ampliﬁed cassette containing igrABCDEF was cloned
downstream of a mycobacterial constitutive promoter in the
shuttle vector pJEB402, which integrates into the phage L5
attachment site [27, 28]. DNA from the resulting plasmid pJC52
was prepared from E. coli transformants, sequenced, and used
to transform H37Rv: Digr.
In vitro characterization of H37Rv: Digr. Hydrogen per-
oxide sensitivity assays were conducted in catalase-free 7H9;
log-phase bacteria were washed and diluted to cfu/mL
61 /H1100310
before exposure to 1 mmol/L H 2O2. T o test nitric oxide (NO)
sensitivity, log-phase bacteria were diluted to an OD 600 of 0.08
and exposed to 3 mmol/L NaNO 2 in acidiﬁed 7H9 as described
elsewhere [29]. Surviving bacteria for both assays were enu-
merated by plating on 7H10. T o test the effect of iron limitation,
log-phase bacteria were diluted to an OD
600 of 0.04 and exposed
to increasing concentrations of 2,2′-dipyridyl (DPI; Sigma) [30].
A modiﬁed 7H9 was used to evaluate growth on limited carbon
sources with substrates added as follows: 10 mmol/L glycerol,
pyruvate, and succinate; 5 mmol/L butyrate, valerate, and iso-
valerate; or 0.25 mmol/L dodecanoate and palmitate and 0.15%
Tween 80 [13]. Growth of bacteria in these assays was assessed
by measuring the optical density at 600 nm. For neutral red
staining, colonies were scraped into polystyrene tubes and pro-
cessed as described elsewhere [31].
Aerosol infection of mice. Mice were infected as described

RESULTS
Transposon library screen identiﬁcation of theigr region. We
previously observed that, although deleting RD1 from wild-
type H37Rv results in attenuation, H37Rv: DRD1 is still more
virulent than the bacille Calmette-Gue ´rin (BCG) vaccine strain
in long-term infection [21, 33]. MTB can kill macrophages in
vitro, and strains that are attenuated in macrophages are often
also attenuated in vivo [21, 24, 34–36]. T o identify genes po-
tentially responsible for the residual virulence of H37Rv:DRD1,
we generated a transposon mutant library in this background
using the transposon donor phagemid MycoMarT7 [22] and
screened for mutants with reduced ability to kill human mac-
rophage–like THP-1 cells.
Approximately 3100 transposon mutants were transferred to
7H9 medium in 96-well plates and used to infect THP-1 mono-
layers, with H37Rv: DRD1 and BCG included as controls for
killing or lack of killing, respectively. Fourteen mutants non-
toxic to THP-1 cells were isolated and rescreened in a 24-well
format. The site of transposon insertion was determined for
the 8 clones that were reproducibly attenuated. Sequencing
revealed that 4 of these had independent insertions in 3 adjacent
genes (ﬁgure 1 A). These genes are 3 of 6 open reading frames
lying in the same orientation and annotated as a cytochrome
P450 (cyp125), 2 acyl–coenzyme A (CoA) dehydrogenases
(fadE28 and fadE29), 2 conserved hypotheticals (Rv3541c and
Rv3542c), and a lipid transfer protein (ltp2).
T o determine whether the attenuation of these transposon
mutants was linked to RD1 and to investigate the role of these

No enhanced inhibition of mutant after macrophage
activation. The addition of IFN- g and LPS to macrophages
induces an activation program that includes the production of
reactive species such as NO and inﬂammatory signaling mol-
ecules, nutrient restriction, and an enhanced ability to kill in-
tracellular pathogens [37], and NO controls the replication of
MTB in murine cells [38]. When J774A.1 murine macrophages
were infected in the absence of IFN- g and LPS pretreatment,
we observed trends similar to those in THP-1 experiments
(ﬁgure 3C). Bacteria in H37Rv- and complement-infected wells
grew by ∼ 27- and ∼ 48-fold, respectively, by day 6, whereas
H37Rv:Digr grew by only ∼ 8-fold. However, when this exper-
iment was repeated with IFN- g– and LPS-stimulated J774A.1
cells, the difference between H37Rv and H37Rv: Digr disap-
peared (ﬁgure 3D ). All 3 strains grew only 5–8-fold over the
course of 6 days, comparable to H37Rv: Digr growth in non-
activated J774A.1 cells. Thus, wild-type and complemented bac-
teria grow well in naive J774A.1 cells, but their growth is re-
stricted in activated cells. By contrast, H37Rv: Digr growth is
restricted even in naive cells, and activation of those cells has
no additional effect.
Characterization of H37Rv: Digr in vitro. Genes of the igr
loci are cotranscribed, and bioinformatics analyses suggest that
at least 3 of 6 genes may be involved in lipid metabolism. T o
determine whether the deletion of these genes affected the lipid-
rich cell walls of H37Rv and H37Rv: Digr in vitro, both strains
were exposed to a variety of stresses. These included several
antimicrobial compounds, acidiﬁed nitrite, and hydrogen per-
oxide. Additionally, we assessed neutral red staining, a phe-
notype that correlates with virulence and the presence of
methyl-branched fatty acids [39]. In every case, the mutant
strain was indistinguishable from the wild type (ﬁgure 4 A, 4B,
and 4G and data not shown).
Previous studies have suggested that host lipids are utilized
by intracellular MTB 10, 12–14]. T o test whether the igr region
is directly involved in fatty acid utilization, we examined growth
on a modiﬁed 7H9 medium supplemented with speciﬁc carbon
sources, including glycerol, pyruvate, succinate, butyrate, val-
erate, isovalerate, dodecanoate, and palmitate (ﬁgure 4 C–4E).
As in our other in vitro assays, we observed no difference
between H37Rv:Digr and the wild type, which suggests that the
ability of this mutant to use these substrates is unaffected.
The host environment is iron limited, and MTB requires
iron for full virulence [30, 40, 41]. Additionally, a gene related
to igrB and igrC, MTB fadE14, has been proposed to function
in mycobactin synthesis [42]. We investigated whether H37Rv:
Digr was deﬁcient in its ability to grow in iron-limited con-
ditions by exposing cultures to the iron chelator DPI. Although
increasing concentrations of DPI produced concomitant re-
ductions in growth, there was no difference between wild-type
and mutant strains (ﬁgure 4 F).

these genes are important in vivo, H37Rv, H37Rv:D igr, and the
complemented mutant were introduced into the lungs of

DISCUSSION
In the present study, we identiﬁed and partially characterized
a region of the MTB genome important for bacterial success
in vivo. The proteins encoded by Rv3540c–RV3545c (renamed
“igrABCDEF” in this study) are predicted to encode a cyto-
chrome P450, 2 FadEs, 2 conserved hypotheticals, and a lipid-
transfer protein. However, we have been unsuccessful at iden-
tifying a mutant phenotype independent of host cells, and the
precise function of these genes remains unclear.
There are scant functional data for the numerous predicted
cytochrome P450s, FadEs, and lipid-transfer proteins encoded

 

794 • JID 2007:196 (1 September) • Chang et al.
by the MTB genome. P450s are monooxygenases that play a
variety of roles, including in detoxiﬁcation, lipid metabolism,
and production of secondary metabolites [47, 48]. FadEs, or
acyl-CoA dehydrogenases, are thought to catalyze the ﬁrst step
of b-oxidation. However, at least one FadE (FadE14) has been
proposed to function in the biosynthesis of the mycobacterial
siderophore mycobactin [42], which underscores the likelihood
that the abundance of fadEs in the MTB genome reﬂects mul-
tiple distinct functions.
Bioinformatics analyses support the role of igr in lipid me-
tabolism. In addition to the putative FadEs (igrB and igrC),
the predicted products of igrE and igrF have similarity to enoyl-
CoA hydratases and the thiolase domain of the mammalian
sterol carrier protein (SCP)–X, respectively; both enzymatic
activities are involved in b-oxidation. Although the precise
function of SCP-X remains unclear, mice lacking the gene ex-
hibit deﬁciencies in the assimilation of the methyl-branched
fatty acids [43, 44]. In addition, a recent report also identiﬁed
igr homologs among the complement of genes up-regulated by
cholesterol in a Rhodococcus species strain RHA1 [45]. Studies
to address the role of igr in the metabolism of these substrates
are ongoing.
Previous whole-genome approaches highlighted that the igr
region is up-regulated in macrophages [18], where it plays an
important role [19], and that this region is required for survival
in mouse spleens after intravenous infection [20]. Consistent
with these data, we found that H37Rv: Digr grew poorly in both
human and murine macrophages. Interestingly, the growth dif-
ference between wild-type and mutant strains disappeared
when macrophages were preactivated with IFN- g and LPS;
growth of H37Rv was checked, but the activation state of the
macrophages had no additional effect on H37Rv: Digr growth.
Although we are unable at present to distinguish between a
replication defect and increased susceptibility to intracellular
killing, our in vitro data suggest that H37Rv:D igr is not more
sensitive to reactive intermediates. Instead, the mutant may be
deﬁcient in accessing a nutrient that wild-type bacteria acquire
from naive macrophages. Activation of the host cell could limit
availability of the nutrient, restricting the growth of H37Rv in
these cells, whereas H37Rv: Digr grows poorly regardless. We
observed no difference in the growth of wild-type and mutant
strains fed various carbon sources or exposed to iron-limited
medium, but it is possible that we have not identiﬁed the rel-
evant nutrient, given that characterization of the complex host
environment remains incomplete. An additional possibility is
that the intracellular growth defect of H37Rv:D igr arises from
the inability to manipulate host responses—for example, by
synthesizing a mycobacterial product such as an immunomod-
ulatory surface lipid or by altering a host lipid important for
infection. The effects of several mycobacterial lipids on host
immune cells have been documented [16, 17], and cholesterol
is a component of host membranes that is essential for MTB
pathogenesis [46].
A second, unexpected observation from these studies was
that, although H37Rv: Digr growth initially lagged in a murine
aerosol infection model, the mutant continued to grow past
the time at which wild-type growth arrested, and this growth
reached numbers comparable to H37Rv in the lungs. Growth
arrest of wild-type bacteria correlates with the onset of adaptive
immunity; in mice, this occurs 20–30 days after aerosol infec-
tion [49]. Previous studies have suggested that the induction
of adaptive immunity depends on the dissemination of bacteria
to the spleen [50]. The appearance of H37Rv:D igr bacilli in this
organ was strikingly delayed, even compared with BCG [21].
Thus, replication of H37Rv: Digr in the lung may proceed past
week 4 because the mutant is less adept at activating adaptive
immunity. Alternatively, the importance of igr may vary during
the course of infection. The initial lag of H37Rv: Digr suggests
that these genes are important early during infection, yet this
mutant clearly persists in the absence of these genes. It is pos-
sible that compensatory mechanisms—perhaps attributable to
the other P450s, FadEs, and lipid transfer proteins—are in-
duced by this time, which allows the bacteria to replicate. Con-
tinued analysis of the igr region will advance our understanding
of the environment faced by this pathogen within host cells.

第2页：双栏材料与方法页，说明菌株培养、转座子筛选、基因删除与互补、巨噬细胞毒性和细胞内生长、小鼠气溶胶感染及组织学方法；表1提示研究使用的引物列表。
第3页：双栏结果页；图1展示igr基因区域、转座子插入位点和RT-PCR产物，图2为确认igr区删除的Southern blot，正文报告减毒突变株的筛选和基因区构建。
第4页：以图表为主的结果页，图3包含多组时间曲线，比较野生型、igr删除株及互补株对THP-1细胞的毒性和在THP-1及J774巨噬细胞中的增殖。
第5页：双栏结果页，图4由多组生长和存活曲线及显微图组成，比较野生型与igr删除株在氧化或硝化应激、不同碳源、铁限制等体外条件下的表型，整体未见相应普遍生长缺陷。
第6页：双栏结果与讨论页；图5展示小鼠肺和脾细菌负荷随时间变化及肺组织病理切片，显示igr删除株早期生长和播散延迟、肺损伤减轻，正文随后进入机制讨论。
第7页：双栏讨论末段，分析cyp125、fadE28、fadE29等基因与脂质代谢和感染阶段特异性表型的关系，随后为致谢和参考文献开端。
第8页：双栏参考文献末页，继续列出结核分枝杆菌细胞内生存、脂质代谢、P450及小鼠感染模型相关文献。
